Fit a bias-corrected synthetic control

Source: R/fit_scm.R
fit_scm.Rd

The Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller synthetic control, matched on an arbitrary predictor matrix rather than on pre-period outcomes alone, with the Abadie-L'Hour / Ben-Michael-Feller-Rothstein bias correction applied on top. This is the estimator Orlova, Rury and Wiltshire (2023) use as their preferred specification, via the Stata package allsynth (Wiltshire 2022); fit_sdid() covers the synthetic-DiD and plain-DiD comparisons they report alongside it.

Usage

fit_scm(
  Y,
  N0,
  T0,
  X = NULL,
  outcome_periods = NULL,
  bias_correct = TRUE,
  bc_ridge = 1e-04,
  bc_donors = c("auto", "positive", "all"),
  v_method = c("equal", "mspe", "synth"),
  v_starts = 8L,
  v_maxit = 1000L,
  penalty = 0
)

Arguments

Y

Outcome matrix, units x periods, controls first and the treated unit last – the layout synthdid::panel.matrices() returns.

N0

Number of control units (the first N0 rows of Y).

T0

Number of pre-treatment periods (the first T0 columns).

X

Optional units x predictors matrix of time-invariant predictors, rows in the same order as Y. Columns that are constant across units are dropped with a warning: they cannot discriminate between donors.

outcome_periods

Integer indices of pre-treatment columns of Y to include as predictors, on top of X. NULL (the default) uses every pre-treatment period. Pass a subset to reproduce a specification that matches on selected pre-treatment years.

bias_correct

Apply the bias correction. TRUE by default.

bc_ridge

Ridge penalty for the bias-correction regressions, on standardised predictors. Small and positive; only binds when the positive-weight donors are few.

bc_donors

Which donors the bias-correction regressions are fitted on. "positive" uses only donors carrying positive weight, as allsynth does; "all" uses the whole pool, as augmented SCM does; "auto" (the default) uses the positive-weight donors when there are comfortably more of them than predictors and falls back to the whole pool otherwise, reporting when it does. The fallback matters: a sparse synthetic control can easily name fewer donors than there are predictors, and the regression is then rank-deficient exactly when the correction is being asked to do the most work.

v_method

How the diagonal of V is chosen. "equal" (default) weights standardised predictors equally. "mspe" searches for the V minimising pre-period MSPE, from v_starts deterministic starting points. "synth" does the "mspe" search AND asks the Synth package for its own solution, then keeps whichever fits the pre-period better – see the note below on why that is not redundant. "synth" needs the suggested Synth package and falls back to "mspe" with a warning if it is missing.

v_starts

Restarts for the "mspe" search, the first from equal weights and the rest scattered. One start is not enough – see the note in the code. Ignored when v_method = "equal".

v_maxit

Nelder-Mead iterations per restart.

penalty

Abadie-L'Hour (2021) penalty lambda, non-negative. Zero (the default) is the classic synthetic control. A positive value adds a charge for each donor's own distance from the treated unit, which makes the weights unique and favours donors that resemble the treated unit individually rather than only on average. Its main use here is breaking ties when the pre-period is fitted exactly: any small positive value then picks, among the exact fits, the one built from the nearest donors. Larger values trade pre-period fit for locality, and as penalty grows the synthetic control becomes the single nearest neighbour. The scale is that of the standardised predictors.

Value

A list with att (mean corrected gap over the post-treatment periods), gap (the corrected gap in every period, named by the columns of Y), gap_raw (before correction), pre_rmspe, post_rmspe, rmspe_ratio (post_rmspe / pre_rmspe), the same three computed on the uncorrected gaps with a _raw suffix – plus rmspe_ratio_hybrid (corrected post over uncorrected pre) – see the code for which to hand rmspe_pvalue() – omega (donor weights, named by the control rownames), v (the predictor weights used), n_predictors, bias_correct, N0 and T0, plus two flags. exact_match is TRUE when the predictors are matched exactly: the weights are then generally not unique and the estimate depends on which optimal weights are returned, so it warns (class sdidlab_exact_fit) unless a penalty is set. exact_fit is TRUE when the whole pre-period is reproduced exactly, which also leaves the RMSPE ratios undefined (NA).

Details

The weight solve is checked against an exact quadratic-programming solution in the test suite: at convergence it reaches the same objective, which is at least as low as Synth's interior-point solve.

It is deliberately separate from fit_sdid() rather than another estimator = branch there. fit_sdid() delegates to synthdid, whose sc_estimate() matches on pre-period outcomes only and has no bias correction; bolting predictor matching onto it would change the meaning of the existing "sc" option and put every stored run's numbers in play.

What the two steps do

Matching. Donor weights w sit on the simplex and minimise \((X_1 - X_0 w)' V (X_1 - X_0 w)\), where the columns of X are the predictors and V is diagonal. Predictors are standardised by their cross-unit standard deviation first, so V = I means "weight every predictor equally after standardisation" – the special case of ADH that does not require the nested optimisation. v_method = "mspe" instead searches over diagonal V for the one minimising pre-period MSPE of the outcome, which is what Synth does by default.

Neither search dominates, which is why "synth" runs both. Synth optimises V with optimx from a single equal-weight start and solves for w with an interior-point QP; this package uses several deterministic starts and an exact active-set solve (see sc_weights_simplex()). The V surface is rough, so the two searches can land in different local minima, and either can find the better one. The objective is the same and is directly comparable, so taking the better of the two is free accuracy and the only defensible default when the surface is this rough.

When several convex combinations of donors fit equally well the minimiser is not unique, and different solvers can return very different comparison groups with the same loss. penalty resolves such ties; without it, report omega rather than assuming it.

Bias correction. Even a good synthetic control leaves a residual discrepancy in the predictors, and that discrepancy biases the estimate. The correction regresses the outcome on the predictors among the donor units, one regression per period, and subtracts the model's prediction of the discrepancy. A ridge penalty keeps it defined when the positive- weight donors are fewer than the predictors.

Note the diagnostic consequence, which is a feature and not a bug: in any period whose outcome is itself a predictor, the corrected gap is mechanically zero, because the period's regression fits that column exactly. Seeing a row of exact zeros in the gap path is confirmation that the correction ran, not evidence of a perfect match. It is what produces the flat segments at matched years in bias-corrected SCM gap figures.

References

Abadie, A., Diamond, A. and Hainmueller, J. (2010). Synthetic Control Methods for Comparative Case Studies. Journal of the American Statistical Association 105(490), 493-505.

Abadie, A. and L'Hour, J. (2021). A Penalized Synthetic Control Estimator for Disaggregated Data. Journal of the American Statistical Association 116(536), 1817-1834.

Ben-Michael, E., Feller, A. and Rothstein, J. (2021). The Augmented Synthetic Control Method. Journal of the American Statistical Association 116(536), 1789-1803.

See also

rmspe_pvalue() for the permutation inference this feeds, fit_sdid() for the synthetic-DiD and DiD comparisons.

Examples

set.seed(1)
Y <- matrix(rnorm(11 * 8), nrow = 11,
            dimnames = list(c(paste0("d", 1:10), "treated"), 2010:2017))
Y[11, 7:8] <- Y[11, 7:8] + 3
fit_scm(Y, N0 = 10, T0 = 6)$att
#> Bias correction fitted on all 10 donors, not the 3 with positive weight.
#> ℹ 6 predictors need more donors than that to be identified.
#> [1] 2.394834
